questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A performance history claim and one production record
questions.learningObjective: Identify the limit of a single production record
questions.stem: During the morning handover on the surgical ward, a nurse claims that the hospital pantomime of 1987 was the first of its kind, offering a single typed programme as proof.

options.text: The claim overreaches, because one production record shows what happened once, not that it happened first
The claim fails only because the typed programme is poorly preserved, so a cleaner copy would settle it
options.misconception: blames the copy condition instead of the claim logic

options.text: The claim cannot be judged, since performance history may never rest on paper records of working ward plays
options.misconception: believes performance history may never use paper records

options.text: The claim is sound, because any surviving programme proves the production was the first of its kind
options.misconception: believes one document can prove a first in a whole tradition

questions.explanation: A single programme records one production, so it cannot show that it was first of its kind. Better preservation would not change that; the claim needs earlier records, not a cleaner copy.
questions.hint: Ask what one record can actually establish.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: What a concept statement argues
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a concept statement is written to do
questions.stem: At the night handover, the ward sister explains why the theatre company's concept statement was written as an argument rather than a description.

answer.exemplar: A concept statement persuades. It selects, emphasises and omits deliberately so that the audience reads the production in a particular way, which is why it is closer to an argument than to a summary of what the evening contains.

questions.explanation: A concept statement persuades, selecting and emphasising to direct the audience's reading of the production. Calling it a description mistakes its purpose, since a plain account would not argue.
questions.hint: Ask what a statement wants the reader to do.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: What a notice holds against a work
questions.learningObjective: Analyse the function of a programme notice
questions.stem: One nurse on the day team asks what a printed programme notice is doing when it holds a production against an older and better known stage version.

options.text: It is simply advertising, because every notice tells the audience what the new production resembles
options.misconception: treats the notice as pure promotion rather than argument

options.text: It is an act of comparison, using a known older work to say what the new staging is worth
It is historical context, since notices exist mainly to explain where the production came from
options.misconception: believes the notice only supplies background and makes no.

options.text: It is a criticism of the past, because a notice measures the new work only against what came before
options.misconception: reads comparison as a verdict on the older work

questions.explanation: Comparing a new staging with a known older version lets the notice use a scale the audience already recognises. Calling it advertising overlooks that the comparison argues about value.
questions.hint: Ask why the older work is the measure chosen.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: An interpretation and the evidence for it
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish support for an interpretation from proof of it

stimulus.body: A note pinned inside a rehearsal folder reads: 'The play is not really about the robbery. Every scene turns on one family member withholding something from another. I have marked six lines that show it.'

questions.stem: Reading the old production file during handover, a nurse concludes that the play's real subject is domestic betrayal and lists the lines that support her.

options.text: Her conclusion is weak, because a reader's preference cannot decide what a play is really about
options.misconception: treats a reader's preference as decisive against any reading

options.text: Her conclusion is weak, because the marked lines prove only that she was paying close attention
options.misconception: thinks careful attention weakens rather than strengthens a.

options.text: Her conclusion is arguable, because the marked lines support her reading but do not rule out others
Her conclusion is sound, because six supporting lines are enough to settle what any play is about
options.misconception: believes a handful of quoted lines settles the meaning of a.

questions.explanation: Marked lines are genuine evidence, so dismissing them as preference understates her case. Equally they support one reading rather than excluding others, and a stronger claim would test rivals.
questions.hint: Weigh support for a reading against proof of it.

questions.topic: Documentary theatre and its question
questions.learningObjective: Formulate the ethical question documentary theatre should put to its audience
questions.stem: Over the ward's early handover, a nurse who helps with a hospital playgroup wonders what question a documentary production should put to the people in the room.

options.text: It should ask whether the testimony is accurate, because accuracy is the first duty of a documentary work
options.misconception: treats truth as the only question a documentary work must.

options.text: It should ask whether the audience is moved, since the point of such a work is the effect it has on the room
options.misconception: assumes the audience response measures a documentary work

options.text: It should ask whether the recording can be improved, because better material makes the fairness question.
options.misconception: believes production quality settles the ethics of.

options.text: It should ask what the production owes the people whose testimony it holds, since watching is not passive

questions.explanation: The productive question concerns the audience's place as viewers of testimony. Asking only whether the material is true narrows the issue to accuracy and ignores how watching acts on people recorded.
questions.hint: Ask what the recording does to the people recorded.

options.misconception: reduces a building influence to its technical equipment

options.text: The claim needs qualification, because proximity offers closeness but the staging decides whether it is felt

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A performance history claim and one production record
questions.learningObjective: Assess what a surviving document can and cannot prove
questions.stem: Two nurses swap notes at the shift change and disagree about what a surviving call sheet can prove about a production's first night.

answer.exemplar: A call sheet fixes who was called, on what date and for which rehearsal or performance, so it can anchor a production in time and in company. It cannot show how the work was received, whether it succeeded, or how it differed from other stagings of the same text.

questions.explanation: A call sheet documents the practical facts of a production's preparation. Treating it as evidence of artistic effect overreads it, since it records names and dates rather than what the audience.
questions.hint: Ask which kind of fact the document records.

The description is unfair, because a concept statement is only a summary of the plot for busy readers
options.misconception: reduces the statement to a plot summary

questions.explanation: A concept statement sets out the reading the production invites, so treating it as a statement about meaning is accurate.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A performance history claim and one production record
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a first performance claim needs more than one record
questions.stem: Before the early handover, a nurse checks a claim that the ward's first 1974 production was also the hospital's first performance of any kind.

answer.exemplar: A first-performance claim is a claim about everything that came before, so it needs evidence of the absence of earlier performances as well as evidence of this one. questions.explanation: The claim concerns a whole prior history, and one dated record can only confirm its own event. The stronger demand for evidence of absence is what the single programme cannot meet on its own.
questions.hint: Ask what the claim must show about everything earlier.

The insistence holds, because only a thrust stage lets actors and audience share the same light
options.misconception: believes shared lighting is the sole route to intimacy

options.text: The insistence is confused, because audiences in a thrust house are always watching from behind one another
options.misconception: assumes thrust audiences always view one another's backs

options.text: The insistence is confused, because intimacy of any kind is a nineteenth-century invention
options.misconception: historicises intimacy as a period fashion

questions.explanation: End-on staging can also be arranged for closeness, so the thrust form offers a possibility rather than a guarantee.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A performance history claim and one production record
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate an overreaching performance history claim
questions.stem: Under pressure at handover, a nurse makes a sweeping claim about performance history from a single surviving programme sheet.

options.text: The claim overreaches, because programme sheets are administrative documents with no artistic content
options.misconception: denies that programmes carry any artistic information

options.text: The claim overreaches, because a single sheet supports one production and cannot carry a history
The claim is fair, because historians often have to work from single fragments and manage perfectly
options.misconception: believes that fragmentary evidence makes any claim safe

options.text: The claim is fair, because the pressure of a busy shift excuses a claim made without checking
options.misconception: lets haste excuse an unsupported claim

questions.explanation: A single sheet supports one production and cannot carry a whole history, so the sweeping claim overreaches. The distracting options fail because fragments still need care.
questions.hint: Ask how much the one sheet can carry.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: What a concept statement argues
questions.learningObjective: Explain the omissions of a concept statement

stimulus.body: A concept statement reads: 'We chose the smaller hall. We chose to keep the interval. Everything else was decided by the play.'

questions.stem: Handing over a complicated shift, a nurse explains the argument a concept statement makes and what it leaves out.

options.text: It argues nothing, because a statement that mentions two choices has no position to defend
options.misconception: believes any restraint means the absence of an argument

options.text: It argues for the season, because the statement is written to defend the choices made to members
options.misconception: reads the statement as a defence of the season

options.text: It argues for restraint, claiming that the play should carry the evening.
It argues for the venue, claiming that the smaller hall is the best room the company has ever used
options.misconception: reads the statement as praise of the hall

questions.explanation: The statement defends restraint and the play's own sufficiency, and its silences about other choices are part of that position.
questions.hint: Ask what the statement declines to discuss.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: What a notice holds against a work
questions.learningObjective: Identify the assumption in a programme notice's comparison

stimulus.body: A programme note reads: 'For those who remember the original, this staging does less, and does it on purpose.'

questions.stem: In the theatre foyer handover, a nurse reads a production notice and asks what the comparison inside it assumes.

options.text: It assumes the reader prefers the original, and that the new staging must apologise for its restraint
options.misconception: presumes the reader's preference and an apology

options.text: It assumes the reader knows the play's plot, since the comparison depends on having read it
options.misconception: treats the comparison as dependent on plot knowledge

options.text: It assumes the reader is a critic, since only critics appreciate a deliberate reduction of material
options.misconception: restricts the note's audience to critics

options.text: It assumes the reader shares a memory of the original staging, and that doing less is a deliberate choice

questions.explanation: The note works because it addresses an audience with a shared memory of the earlier staging and frames reduction as intent.
questions.hint: Ask who the note imagines it is speaking to.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: An interpretation and the evidence for it
questions.learningObjective: Synthesise an interpretation with the evidence that would convince
questions.stem: During the final handover of the shift, a nurse weighs an interpretation against the evidence that would make it convincing.

answer.exemplar: The interpretation becomes convincing when the evidence is matched to the claim it supports, not when more evidence is gathered. A staging detail can show how a reading was produced, and a document can show what was decided, but neither settles a question about the play that only the text's own structure can adjudicate.

questions.explanation: The right test is whether the evidence bears on the claim, not how much of it there is. Gathering more material of the wrong kind leaves the reading exactly where it started.
questions.hint: Ask what kind of claim the evidence can support.
